Question: At the beginning of the school year, \(50\%\) of all students in Mr. Wells’ math class answered “Yes” to the question “Do you love math”, and \(50\%\) answered “No.” At the end of the school year, \(70\%\) answered “Yes” and \(30\%\) answered “No.” Altogether, \(x\%\) of the students gave a different answer at the beginning and end of the school year. What is the difference between the maximum and the minimum possible values of \(x?\)
Solution:
The percentage answering Yes rises from \(50\%\) to \(70\%\), a gain of \(20\%\) of the class. At least that many students must change answers. This minimum is attainable: let \(20\%\) of the class change from No to Yes, and let everyone else keep the same answer. Thus the minimum value of \(x\) is \(20\).

To find the maximum, notice that only \(50\%\) of the class initially answered No. Even if all of them change to Yes, they cannot supply all \(70\%\) of the final Yes answers. At least \(70\%-50\%=20\%\) of the class must answer Yes both times. These students do not change, so at most \(80\%\) can change.

This upper bound is attainable: let all \(50\%\) who initially answered No change to Yes, and let \(30\%\) of the class change from Yes to No. The remaining \(20\%\) keep answering Yes. The final totals are then \(70\%\) Yes and \(30\%\) No, with \(80\%\) changing.

Therefore the requested difference is
\[80-20=\boxed{60},\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
